welcome.lead: OpenCelium connects the systems you already run — Jira, Zendesk, SAP and HubSpot — and keeps their data in sync.
welcome.body: Describe an API once, then connect its methods on a canvas. This tour shows the shortest path from setup to a running workflow.

theme.lightDescription: Best in bright rooms and on projectors.
theme.darkDescription: Easier on the eyes during long sessions.

palette.body: It is highlighted behind this dialog. Press {{key}} + K from any screen to open it — you never have to reach for it with the mouse.
palette.tokensBody: Enter an action, then what it applies to. Start by typing what you want to do.
palette.helpBody: If you forget a command, this is the only one you need to remember.

layers.body: OpenCelium builds an integration in three layers, and each one needs the one before it. The next two steps set up the first layer.
layers.invoker: Describes an API: its endpoints, auth and request shapes. One file, reusable.
layers.connector: One real system: that invoker plus a base URL and credentials.
layers.workflow: The integration itself: methods of as many connectors as you need, wired on a canvas.

invoker.body: An invoker describes one API. Choose the quicker path unless your system requires a custom setup.
invoker.uploadBody: Upload an existing .xml file. Maximum size: 1 GB.
invoker.gitBody: Download the current community library from the OpenCelium repository.
invoker.manualBody: For an API we do not support yet, define its endpoints, authentication and response formats manually.
invoker.existingBody: Your API descriptions are already available, so you can skip the upload task.
invoker.existingList: They are configured and ready, so the upload step will be skipped. You can add more at any time.
invoker.ready: Ready to use in a connector.
invoker.invalidType: Invoker files must use the .xml format.
invoker.tooLarge: The file exceeds the 1 GB limit.

connector.body: A connector is one invoker plus the base URL and credentials of a system you actually run. The wizard walks you through it and tests the connection before saving.
connector.pickInvoker: Pick the invoker to build it from
connector.noInvokers: Add an invoker first — every connector is built from one.

license.body: Every call a workflow makes to a connected system counts as one operation. Activate a license when you need more.
license.actionsBody: Activation, extra operations and offline requests all live on the licence page. Whichever applies to this install is offered there.

header.title: What this page tells you
header.body: A live operational view of this OpenCelium instance: how much is running, how much of it fails, what the machine is spending on it, and which workflows are doing the work. The range beside the title applies to the timeline widgets; the live counters are running totals.

tiles.title: Live counters
tiles.body: These five arrive over the websocket rather than a REST call, so they move while you watch: total executions, the share that failed, average and total run time, and the size of the execution logs on disk. The dot in each corner is the state of that live connection — spinners mean it is still connecting.

executions.title: Executions and failures
executions.body: Two series over the same seven days: every execution, and the failures among them. Hover a day to read the exact counts and that day's failure rate.

resources.title: What it costs the machine
resources.body: CPU load and memory in use, as a share of what this instance has available. Both gauges shift from teal toward red past 60%, so a system under pressure is visible without reading the numbers.

connectors.title: Which workflows are busiest
connectors.body: The five workflows with the most executions in the window, each with its own failure rate. The quickest way to find the one worth opening after a bad night.

comingSoon.title: Not wired up yet
comingSoon.body: These three are greyed out on purpose: the layout is settled but the endpoints behind them are still being built. Nothing here is broken — the cards fill in once the API lands.

createWorkflow.title: Start a new workflow
createWorkflow.body: Opens the visual editor on an empty canvas, where connector methods and if/loop operators are composed into an integration. It is hidden on narrow screens and for roles that may not create connections.

palette.title: The command palette
palette.body: Every action in the app is reachable from here — press {{key}} + K from anywhere to focus it. Commands read verb first (create connector, list schedules), and typing help lists the whole tree.

language.title: English or German
language.body: Switches the interface language straight away. The choice is saved onto your account as well as this browser, so it follows you to another machine.

help.title: Help, and this tour
help.body: Two entries behind this icon: the OpenCelium documentation at docs.opencelium.io, which opens in a new tab, and Start tour — which is how you get back to this walkthrough later.

menuSwitch.title: Main and admin menus
menuSwitch.body: The sidebar has two: the main menu for day-to-day work, and the admin menu for users, roles and system settings. Switching lands you on the page you last had open in that menu.

profile.title: Your account
profile.body: Your own details, the permissions your roles grant you, and a password change.

intro.title: Build a working workflow, step by step
intro.body: This short, hands-on tutorial walks the whole editor — methods, a loop, a condition, references and a live test run — built against two invented systems, so nothing you do here is saved. Each step tells you exactly what to do next; follow the pill.

customers.title: List the customers
customers.body: Add getCustomers from Tutorial CRM. It returns every customer with their email, first name and last name. Both systems here are invented — nothing you build is saved.

loop.title: Repeat per customer
loop.body: getCustomers returns a list, so the rest of the workflow has to run once per entry. Use the + after it to add a loop operator.
loop.note: Add a loop operator to continue

iterate.title: Tell the loop what to iterate
iterate.body: A loop on its own does not know what it is walking. Right-click it, open Configuration, and choose the for operator — it iterates an array. Then set its argument to a reference: getCustomers, then customers, then The whole array. Save it, and the loop variable i becomes the customer of the current iteration.

lookup.title: Look each one up, inside the loop
lookup.body: Use the + below the loop, not the one after it — below puts the step inside the loop's scope, at index 1_0, where each iteration has a customer to work with. After the loop it would be step 2 and run just once. Add getClientByEmail from Tutorial Support Desk.
lookup.note: Add the method under the loop to continue

endpoint.title: A reference in the endpoint
endpoint.body: Right-click getClientByEmail, choose Edit URL, then Insert Reference. Pick getCustomers as the method, then build the field path in three picks: customers, then (i loop), then email. Taking (i loop) rather than a fixed element is what ties the reference to the loop, so it resolves to a different customer on each iteration.
endpoint.note: Insert the reference, then close the dialog

branch.title: Only when it is missing
branch.body: Use the + after getClientByEmail to add an IF operator — still inside the loop — and set its condition on the lookup's response: found is false.
branch.note: Add an IF operator to continue

condition.title: Compare the two emails
condition.body: Double-click the IF to open its condition, then Add Condition. Both sides are references: on the left take getClientByEmail's client.email, on the right getCustomers' customers[i].email — the same loop-scoped path as the endpoint. Set the operator to Not equal, so the true branch means this customer has no account yet. Save it.

create.title: Create the missing client
create.body: Use the + below the IF: that is its true branch. Add createClient from Tutorial Support Desk, so it runs once for every customer that was not found — and never for one that was.
create.note: Add the method under the IF to continue

username.title: Two references, one field
username.body: Open createClient's body and find username. Hover its row and press the reference icon, then pick getCustomers, customers, (i loop), firstName. Do it again for lastName. Two references in one field are wrapped in an enhancement automatically — unfold Variable Information to see them listed as VAR_0 and VAR_1, in that order. Join them with a space in the script, then close the dialog.
username.note: Add both references, unfold the variables, edit the script, then close

testrun.title: Run it, without running it
testrun.body: Press play on the start node and choose Debug mode. The run streams its log lines as fast as the engine produces them, and the canvas replays them at a pace you can follow — a dot travels the edge, then the step it feeds lights up. Nothing leaves the browser: the two invented systems answer from fixtures.

pause.title: Freeze the replay
pause.body: The debug controls sit top left, beside the zoom buttons. Pause stops the replay exactly where it is — the run itself carries on in the background, its lines just queue up behind the pause. The log panel opens the tree down to the element you stopped on, so you can read how far the run had got.

step.title: One line at a time
step.body: Stepping applies exactly the next queued line and stays paused. Walk the loop entry, the lookup, the IF's verdict and the create one press at a time: each step moves the token to a single element, so you see the order the engine really took rather than the order the graph is drawn in.

iteration.title: Jump to another pass
iteration.body: Paused inside a loop, the loop node shows which iteration it is on. The skip icon fast-forwards past the rest of the current one and re-pauses as the next begins; typing a number in the counter aims at that iteration instead. Watch the IF change its verdict — one of these customers already has an account.
iteration.note: Skip to the next iteration to continue

speed.title: Set the pace
speed.body: The slider scales every dwell in the replay, including one already mid-wait. The Live toggle in the log panel's header drops the pacing altogether and shows each line the instant it arrives — right for a long run you only want the outcome of, and the reason the debug controls disappear while it is on.

logs.title: Read the run
logs.body: This is the same tree stored runs are shown in. A method row opens to its request and response, a loop row pages through its iterations, an IF row names the branch it took. All of it came from the graph you built — compare createClient's payload against the script you wrote for it.

summary.title: That is a working workflow
summary.body: getCustomers lists everyone, the loop walks them one at a time, getClientByEmail asks the second system about the current customer by reference, the IF lets only the unknown ones through, and createClient fills its fields from the customer being walked. Methods, scope, references, enhancements — every real integration is these four ideas, and the test run is how you check them before anything is scheduled. Nothing here was saved; build the same shape with your own connectors.
summary.note: Invented connectors, so there is nothing to keep

checklist.title: Setup
checklist.dismissBody: It will not come back. You can still restart the tour from the palette with help onboarding, or turn it back on in /ui/config.
